title: Number Equal to Its Divisor Sum
statement: You get a positive integer num. Add up all of its positive divisors except num itself. Return true if that sum equals num, and false otherwise.

examples.why: 1 has no divisors smaller than itself, so the sum is 0. Starting the sum at 1 for every number would wrongly say true.

hints: Checking every number below num is too slow for 10⁸. Divisors come in pairs. How?
If d divides num, so does num / d, and one of the two is at most √num.
Walk d from 2 while d · d ≤ num, adding d and num / d for each divisor (only once when they are equal). Start the sum at 1, but handle num = 1 separately.

explain.intuition:
Divisors come in pairs: if d divides num, so does num / d. In each pair one member is at most √num. So walking d from 2 up to √num finds every divisor, and each hit gives you two at once. For 10⁸ that is 10 000 steps instead of 10⁸.

Two details: when d · d = num the pair is one number, so add it once; and the divisor 1 pairs with num itself, which is excluded, so start the sum at 1 and skip that pair. That trick is wrong for num = 1, whose excluded-self sum is 0.
steps: Set sum = 1 (the divisor 1; its partner is num itself).
For d = 2 while d · d ≤ num: if num % d === 0, add d, and add num / d if it differs from d.
pitfalls: Adding the square root twice for a perfect square like 16.
Returning true for 1 because the sum was started at 1.
Looping all the way to num / 2. It is correct but does 5·10⁷ steps for the largest input.

solutions.title: Divisor pairs up to the square root
solutions.idea: Every divisor d ≤ √num comes with its partner num / d. Sum both, add a square root once, and leave out num itself.

solutions.title: Euclid–Euler: the list is tiny
solutions.idea: Every even number with this property has the form 2^(p−1) · (2^p − 1) with 2^p − 1 prime, and no odd one is known (none exists below 10³⁰⁰). Below 10⁸ there are exactly five.

followups: Return the sum of proper divisors for every number from 1 to n at once. (Hint: a sieve that adds d to all its multiples.)
How would you find all such numbers below 10¹⁸ without checking each one?
